prize_parts.citation: For showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting shape international trade, productivity and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: Firm heterogeneity and selection moved trade analysis from industries and countries to firms. It explains who exports, who invests abroad, how openness reallocates resources toward more productive firms, and why gains from trade take a particular form. The contribution is conceptual and also measurable. It reorganised how firm-level and transaction-level data are used in trade, and it spread to industrial organisation and macroeconomics. The framework has been tested for more than two decades across countries and datasets. It also complements the 2008 recognition of new trade theory rather than repeating it. Melitz (2003) is the core model, and Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI is a direct extension, so the two-name attribution is concentrated and defensible.
statement.case_against: The attribution boundary is the main weakness. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum contributed firm-level empirical and quantitative foundations that overlap with the Melitz framework but are not among the credited names for this ballot entry. A prize limited to Melitz and Helpman could be read as under-crediting the empirical origins. Some welfare conclusions also depend on parametric assumptions, such as Pareto productivity distributions. Helpman is credited on a second candidate (B001), so the Committee would also have to decide which body of his work it is recognising.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B001 first. He sees Grossman-Helpman as the canonical framework for how organised interests shape trade policy, with a clean two-person attribution, and he notes that trade has had no prize since 2008.
responses.response: I agree that the attribution is cleaner than for B020 and that the framework is foundational. The absence of a trade prize since 2008 is an argument for the field, not for a particular candidate. It applies equally to B020. On the substantive question, the empirical record you acknowledge as mixed matters to me more. Protection-for-sale is a deep theoretical account, but its central predictions have not been confirmed as consistently as the selection and reallocation mechanisms. Those have been checked against firm-level data in many countries and have changed how trade is estimated and how policy is evaluated. That is why I place B001 below B020. I still regard it as a serious alternative.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B001 first for its explanatory framework and durable influence. She notes that Helpman's firm-heterogeneity work also appears on the list, which adds to the case for him.
responses.response: Helpman's presence in both entries does show his stature, but it should not decide which achievement the Committee honours. I read the two strands as distinct contributions. I would not stack them for one person. The question is which strand has had the larger effect on what economists know and measure. I think that is firm heterogeneity, because it changed empirical practice as well as theory. I accept your caution that the political-economy mechanisms are more mixed empirically than their theoretical influence suggests. That caution supports my ordering.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B020 first and proposes Helpman and Melitz. He flags that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are close contributors outside the credited list, and that Redding's quantitative and spatial work extends the core.
responses.response: I share your reading of the core and your concern about the credit boundary. I would not add Redding, because his contribution is later and extends a framework already established. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are harder. Their empirical and quantitative contributions are real, but the conceptual model of selection is most clearly Melitz's. Helpman's extension to exporting versus FDI is the natural second name. I acknowledge that this is a judgement about which contribution to credit, not an uncontested fact, and I would want the Scientific Background to describe the empirical precursors fully.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B020 first. She stresses that it changed both theory and empirical practice and that the field has not been recognised since 2008, so the timing is mature. She also asks whether the Committee might prefer Helpman paired with Grossman.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the combination of conceptual and empirical influence. On your open question, a Helpman-Grossman prize and a Helpman-Melitz prize are different judgements about which discovery matters most. They are not interchangeable. I would not seek a compromise that merges them, and I would not use the breadth of support for B001 as evidence of its scientific weight. If the Committee does prefer B001, I could accept it, but I think the case for B020 is stronger on empirical confirmation.

uncertainties: Whether Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum should be treated as co-originators, which would change the credit boundary.
Whether the Committee wants to recognise Helpman for the firm-heterogeneity strand or the political-economy strand, since he is credited in both.
How robust the welfare conclusions are to parametric assumptions about productivity distributions.
My knowledge of priority claims comes from memory and is not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific connection is apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in industrial organisation and international trade (pricing, exchange-rate pass-through, invoicing currency), which is thematically close to the trade candidates (B020, B001) and to the IO candidate B041. I judge them on the common criteria. I co-authored a 2026 paper with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen, and neither is a candidate on the shortlist. My spouse's public political role is noted as a public fact only, and nothing in the profile suggests it bears on any shortlisted candidate.
